item.title: China’s Weak Soybean Demand Dims Prospects for U.S. Cargoes After Tariff Snub
item.description: By Ella Cao and Naveen Thukral China’s soybean buying is likely to decline in the months ahead due to weak animal feed demand and negative crush margins, leaving little room for US cargoes as they were excluded from proposed tariff relief after last week’s Washington …
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded:
By Ella Cao and Naveen Thukral

China’s soybean buying is likely to decline in the months ahead due to weak animal feed demand and negative crush margins, leaving little room for US cargoes as they were excluded from proposed tariff relief after last week’s Washington summit.

China is set to lower tariffs on a broad range of U.S. farm products, but soybeans, its biggest U.S. agricultural import, were excluded from the tariff-reduction list following talks between Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump.

Private oilseed processors in China, the world’s biggest soybean importer, have covered most of their needs through the Lunar New Year in early February with supplies from Brazil, Argentina and state reserves, traders and crushers said.

“We have booked for all of October and much of November shipments from Brazil and Argentina,” said a senior executive at a Chinese oilseed processing company.

“Most of these cargoes will arrive around the high-demand Chinese New Year period. We are not interested in making further purchases as these will incur losses.”

Chinese state-run companies have bought around 13.7 million metric tons of US soybeans, which are currently being harvested, following a trade deal between the two countries in May, three Asia-based agricultural traders said on condition of anonymity.

However, private crushers have taken only South American shipments, the traders said.

U.S. soybeans still face an additional 10% tariff since the start of last year’s trade war between Beijing and Washington, making them uneconomical for commercial buyers.

Brazilian soybeans were quoted this week at par with U.S. cargoes, excluding the tariffs, at around $590 per ton, including cost and freight, according to the senior Chinese crushing executive and an Asian-based trader.

Brazilian beans typically have a higher oil content, making them more attractive to crushers, they said.

Benchmark Chicago soybean futures are down 1.5% so far this week, with the market expected to face further losses as the U.S. harvest nears its peak and China is set to slow purchases.

Sluggish Demand, Weak Margins

Crushing margins for soybeans scheduled for November shipment from the U.S. Pacific Northwest and the US Gulf are 120 yuan ($17.90) to 200 yuan ($29.83) per ton in the red and about minus 120 yuan per ton for Brazilian soybeans, said Rosa Wang, an analyst at Shanghai JC Intelligence.

Crushers in China’s main processing hub of Rizhao were losing 33.54 yuan per ton of soybeans processed on Tuesday, according to LSEG data.

Import demand has weakened as crushing plants hold high inventories and anticipate softer fourth-quarter feed demand, with sow herds shrinking amid government efforts to curb overcapacity in the hog industry.

Soybean inventories at 111 Chinese crushing plants reached 7.96 million tons in the week of September 25, according to consultancy Mysteel, the highest in at least 15 years.

In Sinograin’s latest auction of imported soybeans, only 37.3% of the 514,000 tons offered were sold, Mysteel data showed, underscoring weak buying appetite in the market.

Chinese buyers booked around 50 soybean cargoes in the first three weeks of September, the fewest in four years, said Eduardo Vanin, senior agriculture strategist at Marex in Curitiba, Brazil, adding that state-run COFCO and Sinograin accounted for about 30 U.S. cargoes, while private buyers booked the rest from Brazil and Argentina.

“Unless margins recover, commercial buyers are unlikely to book more cargoes from overseas,” said Johnny Xiang, founder of Beijing-based AgRadar Consulting.

“If supplies tighten, buyers are more likely to turn to reserve auctions or idle plants for maintenance than import more beans.”

item.title: A Lapel Pin Fuels Chinese Talk of a China-Russia-Iran Triangle
item.description: In China’s tightly managed political information environment, seemingly trivial interactions between senior officials can become material for close reading. Netizens and commentators scrutinize seconds-long clips — who smiles, who initiates a handshake, how firmly leaders grip hands or whether they appear unusually relaxed around one …
item.dc:creator: Rudy Lu
item.content:encoded:
In China’s tightly managed political information environment, seemingly trivial interactions between senior officials can become material for close reading. Netizens and commentators scrutinize seconds-long clips — who smiles, who initiates a handshake, how firmly leaders grip hands or whether they appear unusually relaxed around one another — for clues about relationships that official readouts rarely reveal.

A brief encounter between the foreign ministers of China, Russia and Iran at the BRICS summit has become the latest example.

Video from the sidelines of the summit in New Delhi showed Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi chatting and laughing with his Russian and Iranian counterparts Sergei Lavrov and Abbas Araghchi. At one point, Wang reached toward a pin on Araghchi’s jacket, prompting the Iranian foreign minister to laugh.

Araghchi’s official Telegram channel later posted a close-up of the exchange , identifying the pin as an emblem depicting the map of Iran.

The moment quickly spread across Chinese social media, landing on the trending search list of Weibo, a Chinese social media platform often compared to X, under “Wang Yi helps the Iranian foreign minister straighten his pin” (#王毅帮伊朗外长整理胸针).

A wave of Chinese-language amplification followed.

Nationalist commentary account Rongping (戎评) described Iran as “holding the advantage” and in high spirits, with China and Russia sharing the mood.

“Such a personal and warm interaction between the Chinese and Iranian foreign ministers sends a strong signal to the outside world: China-Iran relations have long gone beyond a simple exchange of interests, and the two sides share a high degree of familiarity and trust,” it wrote.

Another online commentary said the seemingly insignificant gesture reflected a shift in the international balance of power that would make the White House “deeply uncomfortable.”

“U.S. pressure is pushing the three sides closer together,” it said. “Washington can continue to pressure the three countries separately, but it will find it increasingly difficult to stop them from exchanging resources, coordinating positions and jointly seeking alternatives.”

It said Beijing could keep channels open to Gulf Arab countries, and Moscow could draw on its close strategic ties with Tehran. Working through BRICS, the three could help Iran break its diplomatic isolation and avert a complete rupture with the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf states.

Those interpretations, however, largely reflect one strand of domestic online opinion that is sympathetic to Iran and distrustful of the United States. Beijing’s official posture has been more carefully calibrated, especially ahead of Xi Jinping’s scheduled Sept. 24 meeting with Trump in Washington.

Araghchi traveled to Beijing on Sep. 16 for talks with Wang Yi. The Chinese Foreign Ministry described Iran as a “comprehensive strategic partner” and said Beijing was prepared to help safeguard Tehran’s “legitimate rights and interests.”

But much of Wang’s message focused on containing the conflict. He urged Iran and the United States to exercise restraint and return to negotiations, backed dialogue between Tehran and Gulf Arab governments, called for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and warned against the fighting spreading toward Yemen and the Red Sea.

China’s balancing role was also evident when Saudi Arabia asked Beijing to press Iran to rein in the Houthis, Reuters reported, citing three Iranian sources . China then privately urged Tehran to use its influence over the Yemeni group, whose advances threatened Saudi oil exports and shipping through the Red Sea — a vital route for Chinese trade.
